messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Valentina is a 47-year-old Salvadoran American woman who has been married for nineteen years and works as a social ministry worker at a Catholic community center in her city. She came to the intake session speaking quietly, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and described herself as someone who used to believe that helping others was the purpose that held her life together. That sense of purpose, she said, now feels like something she is only performing.

Approximately eight months ago, Valentina was raped by a man she had known professionally — a contractor who had been doing repair work at the community center. The assault occurred in the late afternoon, in a storage room at the back of the building, after the rest of the staff had left. What she remembers is not a continuous event but a series of frozen frames: the overhead light flickering, the sound of tools being set down on a metal shelf, the particular quality of silence that filled the room just before he moved toward her. That silence — thick, suspended, wrong — is the detail that has lodged most deeply in her nervous system. She has no fluid narrative of what happened. She told the clinician that she knows what occurred but cannot find the words to describe it, as though language itself has been revoked. When she tries to recall it, what surfaces are those still images, and with them, an immediate and overwhelming wave of guilt — a conviction that she should have left earlier, should have known, should have done something different.

Those guilt-saturated memories have fed directly into the beliefs that now organize her daily life. Valentina has come to feel that she deserves to suffer for what happened, a punishment logic she applies with quiet consistency. She restricts her eating carefully, finding in that control something that feels like the only domain in which she has agency. She avoids anything that would allow her body or mind to soften — rest, leisure, stillness — because relaxing feels to her not like safety but like exposure, like lowering a guard she cannot afford to lower. These strategies, in turn, have kept the memories from being processed in any narrative or integrated way; by never allowing herself to settle, she ensures that the frozen images remain exactly as they were, unexamined and uncontextualized, ready to resurface.

The memories also sustain a vigilance that has become exhausting. Valentina now experiences the silence of a room — any room, including the office where she meets with community members in need — as a signal that something dangerous is about to happen. When a colleague is late returning from lunch, or when a meeting runs past its scheduled time, she assumes something terrible is unfolding. She cannot relax even when she knows, intellectually, that she is safe. This chronic threat state has in turn reinforced her appraisals: she has concluded that the world is genuinely dangerous, that her perception of threat is accurate rather than distorted, and that she was foolish ever to have believed otherwise. The hypervigilance and the beliefs tighten around each other — the threat confirms the appraisals, and the appraisals confirm the threat — and her strategies of restriction and refusal to rest keep both elevated, preventing any disconfirmation from reaching her.

The appraisals themselves have become their own source of suffering. Valentina describes having lost her faith — in people, in the Church she served, in God — and says that the woman she was before, someone she remembers as genuinely happy, feels like a stranger. She carries a deep shame about what happened to her body, a shame she has not disclosed to her husband, who knows only that she has been "going through something." The distance this has created in their marriage is one of the concrete consequences she named: they no longer sleep easily beside each other, and she has declined every invitation to social gatherings their parish community organizes.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when she froze completely in the doorway of the storage room — now used by a different staff member — and could not move for several minutes. A colleague witnessed it. She is most afraid, she said, that she will never be able to do her work with full presence again. What she is hoping for, more quietly, is to find words for what happened.
